body: Good catch! Not sure if we can fix this without making parsing slower for everybody not messing with locales.

One option to mitigate the issue would be to pin the thread-local locale using `uselocale` (POSIX) / [`_configthreadlocale`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-runtime-library/reference/configthreadlocale?view=msvc-170) (Windows) and change it back afterwards. I'm assuming that's what you have in mind as a "slower" option? For reference, I've confirmed that this works and it's probably the [mitigation](https://github.com/jgreitemann/json-locale-bug-repro/compare/mitigation) I'll end up going with in production (where I can take the liberty to only do this once on the JSON-parsing worker thread, so the perf impact is amortized).

Another option could be to use the extended locale support (`xlocale(3)`) function `strtod_l` afforded by glibc, FreeBSD, Darwin, ... (but crucially not musl AFAICT) and its Windows counterpart [`_strtod_l`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-runtime-library/reference/strtod-strtod-l-wcstod-wcstod-l?view=msvc-170). These work by passing the locale explicitly without changing global state. The locale needs to be allocated by `newlocale`/[`_create_locale`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/c-runtime-library/reference/strtod-strtod-l-wcstod-wcstod-l?view=msvc-170), though, but this can probably be done once in a static? I would hope that this doesn't perform worse compared to `strtod` but haven't tested it yet.

If the extended locale support is not available, would you prefer to fall back to the current implementation and document the safety requirements w.r.t. locale for other platforms or go with the `uselocale` solution? The latter approach would avoid the UB/TOCTOU for _all_ users and (hopefully) potentially only regress on perf for users on platforms without extended locale support.

Lastly, `std::from_chars<double>` in C++17 is locale-independent and generally performs better than `strtod`. It could be used as an alternative implementation when C++17 support is detected. This can be combined with the above approaches to further reduce the share of users potentially affected by UB/TOCTOU or perf regressions.

Let me know which approaches you think are viable, then I can prepare a patch and perform some benchmarks.

> Additionally, changing locale in parallel with locale-dependent functions like strtod() is undefined behavior. Since JSON itself does not allow for decimal separators other than ., it is quite surprising that json::parse() exhibits the same safety issue and should be document if it cannot be avoided.

So the simplest method would be to explicitly document that this library uses locale-specific functions in `parse()`, so changing the locale in parallel with a `parse()` call can cause undefined behavior.  That's not great, so I think pursuing other methods is worthwhile.


At least there is only one line where it calls the overload set of functions `strtof` that chooses `std::strtof`, `std::strtod` or `std::strtold` based on the output type, so at least that changes would be localized.  You'd need to remove the replacement of the decimal point, but that would be a good thing IMHO.

I think falling back to the `_l` family is good when they're available.  From what I've been able to see, the `_l` performance is the same as non-`_l` for single threaded apps, and better for multi-threaded apps, presumably because non-`_l` gets the current locale and calls `_l`, or at least the same helper function that `_l` calls.

I am not the maintainer, so @nlohmann has the final say, but I think this would be a good preference order:
* std::from_chars
* strtod_l
* strtod with the replacement of the decimal point

This would need to be detected in a way that allows determining whether or not the decimal point replacement is needed.  It could be that the decimal point replacement code remains unconditionally, and it's just always populated with `'.'` when `from_chars` or `strtod_l` is used.

> At least there is only one line where it calls the overload set of functions `strtof` that chooses `std::strtof`, `std::strtod` or `std::strtold` based on the output type, so at least that changes would be localized.

The integer parsing functions `std::strtoll` and `std::strtoull` are also used which are also locale-dependent to cover things like thousands separators. Aside from the uses by the lexer, `std::strtoull` is also [used](https://github.com/nlohmann/json/blob/d10879bca8f0aa790105446075a9525b34a3f718/include/nlohmann/detail/json_pointer.hpp#L271) to parse JSON pointers.

Since integers don't have a decimal point and JSON doesn't allow for thousands separators (and the lexer's state machine precludes them), there is no TOCTOU issue for integers. However, changing locale from another thread while these functions are called is still UB, so the fix should probably also cover those functions as well.

>However, changing locale from another thread while these functions are called is still UB, so the fix should probably also cover those functions as well.

I am personally less worried about that, but if it's a simple fix, then it may be worth it.
I think it's a good idea to use `std::from_chars` where it's available. Also `strtod_l`. The question is how reliable we can detect these.

`std::from_chars` could potentially be detected using the feature-test macro `__cpp_lib_to_chars` ([Godbolt](https://godbolt.org/z/zxx4dqT97)). Feature testing is itself a C++20 feature but by the looks of it, it also works when C++20-ready compilers are put in C++17 mode, but not in C++14 mode. However, this would leave a few false negatives, e.g. GCC 10 doesn't know about feature testing so it comes back "Not supported", even in C++17 mode. I think that would be fine since it's an optimization anyway and I suspect the demographic that uses C++17 but doesn't update their toolchain is (hopefully) quite small? Should we also include a macro to forcefully enable/disable the `from_chars` path?

`strtod_l`/`_strtol` could be detected by SFINAE since there are no additional includes necessary.

I'll cook up a PR for this on the weekend to see how this would work out.
Sounds good.  I think the hardest part is going to be setting a flag that says whether or not to get the decimal point from the locale depending on whether or not `strtod_l` is available.

Just a quick heads-up: I have it mostly working now but I want to polish a few things before opening a (draft) PR. I'm a bit pressed for time, so it could be a couple of weeks. I'd expect there will be an ensuing fight with CI until all platforms/compilers are happy.

The `std::from_chars` feature detection turned out to be a bit of a pain because libc++ added floating point support for `std::from_chars` only recently and with the notable omission of the `long double` overload.

The SFINAE-based detection of extended locale support I got working. One surprise was that musl does in fact define `strtof_l` and friends for glibc compatibility but ignores the locale argument and merely delegates to `strtof`. Fortunately, if I understood correctly, musl doesn't let you set different `LC_NUMERIC` locales, so that's not an issue. There doesn't seem to be a dedicated musl CI workflow; I wonder if it would be worth adding that?

I can also confirm that integer parsing (via `strtol` et al.) indeed suffers from UB when switching locale concurrently. Where my original reproduction mostly triggered the assert and only sometimes crashed, a modified version with only an integer field in the JSON object "reliably" reproduces SIGSEGV on Linux and macOS (since there's no TOCTOU race to trip over first). On Windows, the global locale is apparently protected by a mutex, so no crash there, but perf is noticeably degraded. Therefore, my aim would be to expand the fix to also cover integer parsing once I got it working for the floats.
I'd like to work on this as my first contribution, is it still open?
